title: U.S. further restricts China's access to AI chips in wake of Nvidia scandal
summary: The Trump administration on Monday issued a rule that will further restrict China's access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia, just as U.S. President Donald Trump began a trip to China…

image.caption: The motherboard of a laptop containing Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip stands on display at a Microsoft event in San Francisco on Oct. 7, 2026. (Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters)

blocks.text: The Trump administration on Monday issued a rule that will further restrict China's access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia, just as U.S. President Donald Trump began a trip to China to meet with President Xi Jinping.
Move comes as Trump set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping

The new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres in countries like Malaysia and Thailand will hurt Chinese companies that use those data centres to access advanced chips to train their artificial intelligence models.

The new rule shows the Commerce Department is scrambling to show it's cracking down on Chinese access to sensitive U.S. technology, following reporting that the agency turned a blind eye to the smuggling of advanced Nvidia AI chips into China and failed to curb Chinese access to overseas data centres that allowed users to circumvent the restrictions.

Trump is set on Thursday to meet with Xi in China's southern city of Shenzhen, the site of this week's APEC summit. Trump often unleashes punitive tech threats or action against Beijing ahead of such meetings.

The new rule also requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for U.S. export licences for advanced chips, citing the five countries as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of illegally diverting the chips to China.
Lutnick faces scrutiny over Nvidia spy scandal
Lutnick with Trump on China visit

The commerce secretary is going with Trump to China, an indication the president still supports Lutnick, who has come under intense pressure for not taking action in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation last week.
Huang stepped down after admitting to an affair with an executive at Singapore-based cloud company and Nvidia partner Megaspeed.

"The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Commerce Department said in a statement.

blocks.text: The statement said the rule was written by the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council, which also directed its release.
The new restrictions will not apply to systems used by online retailers and social media companies, which the department said do not pose the same national security threat.
They also formally rescind the Biden-era rule that limited global access to AI chips through licensing requirements.

The Commerce Department said in early 2025 that it would not enforce the rule, and would rescind and replace it. But it did not take action until Monday, allowing billions of dollars' worth of restricted Nvidia chips to flow to data centres used by Chinese AI companies.
